core: what a mutual fund is: a pooled investment — an investment company that gathers money from many investors and invests it in a portfolio of securities, managed by professionals (working definition attributed to SEC Investor.gov)
how it works: many investors' money pooled into one portfolio; a manager selects and adjusts the holdings; each share represents part ownership of the whole portfolio
the benefits named: instant diversification (sibling topic referenced only), professional management, access (low minimums, redeemable shares) — one line each
the costs named: management fees and expense ratios — each named generally, stated factually
funds vs individual stocks: a basket of many securities vs a single share of one company (stocks is a sibling topic)
index funds named: funds that follow a passive strategy designed to match a market index, typically with lower fees — one factual line
honest framing: a mutual fund is convenience with a fee; not FDIC-insured, value can fall, past performance does not predict future returns
supporting: net asset value (NAV) as the price at which fund shares are bought and redeemed
shares are bought from and redeemed by the fund itself, on any business day
actively managed funds named for contrast with index funds, one line
no fund guarantees a fixed return; all funds carry risk

claims.claim: A mutual fund is an investment company that pools money from many investors and invests it in a portfolio of securities such as stocks and bonds; the combined holdings are its portfolio, managed by a professional adviser. This is the working definition the lesson adopts, attributed to SEC Investor.gov.
Each mutual fund share represents part ownership of the fund's portfolio and of the gains and losses the portfolio generates.

Investor.gov names professional management, diversification, low minimum investment, and liquidity as the standard features that make mutual funds popular; the lesson names three of them (instant diversification, professional management, access) with one line each.
A mutual fund's portfolio is managed by an investment adviser registered with the SEC, who decides what the fund holds and adjusts it over time.

Funds pass their operating costs to investors by deducting fees and expenses from the portfolio; the management fee is paid out of fund assets to the investment adviser, and the expense ratio expresses total annual fund operating expenses as a percentage of the fund's average net assets.
Even small differences in fees can mean large differences in returns over time, and a fund with high costs must perform better than a low-cost fund to generate the same returns for investors.
An index fund follows a passive investment strategy designed to aim at roughly the return of a particular market index before fees, typically with lower fees than actively managed funds.
Mutual funds are not guaranteed or insured by the FDIC or any other government agency, investors may lose some or all of their money, and past performance does not predict future returns.
Mutual fund shares are bought from and redeemed by the fund itself at the next calculated net asset value on any business day, rather than traded between investors on an exchange.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether index funds or actively managed funds are the better investment
positions: Investor.gov notes index funds typically carry lower fees and fewer transaction costs because they track an index passively.
Investor.gov notes actively managed funds seek to outperform their benchmark but their performance depends heavily on the skill of the manager.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states only the factual mechanics (index funds track an index, typically with lower fees) and does not rank one strategy above the other; no performance advice is given.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a mutual fund's diversification makes it safe
positions: Investor.gov notes that holding a range of companies and industries helps lower risk if one company fails.
Investor.gov also states funds are not guaranteed or insured by the FDIC or any government agency and investors may lose some or all of their money.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents diversification as risk-reducing but not risk-removing, and pairs every benefit with the honest frame that funds can lose value.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate (a 'foundational concept' framing and a toolbox-drawer analogy) with no substantive claims about mutual funds; nothing from it was carried into the lesson.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generated draft entirely: the working definition is now attributed to SEC Investor.gov, the pooled-mechanics are stated explicitly, benefits and costs are named from the source pages, and the honest framing (convenience with a fee, no guarantees) is stated plainly.

sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator investor-education site). Fetched live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: the working definition (a mutual fund is an SEC-registered open-end investment company that pools money from many investors and invests it in stocks, bonds, short-term money-market instruments, other securities or assets, or a combination; the combined holdings are its portfolio, managed by an SEC-registered investment adviser); each share representing part ownership of the portfolio and its gains and losses; the named benefits (professional management, diversification, low minimum investment, liquidity); the three ways investors earn (dividend payments, capital gains distributions, increased net asset value); shares bought from and redeemed by the fund at the next calculated NAV on any business day; funds not guaranteed or insured by the FDIC or any government agency and the possibility of losing some or all of the money invested; past performance not predicting future returns; index funds as a passive strategy designed to achieve approximately the same return as a particular index before fees, typically with lower fees than actively managed funds. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.
